mcqs.question: Why does a min-stack push `(value, min_so_far)` pairs instead of just storing the value and computing the minimum on demand?
options: Storing the minimum-as-of-each-push lets `get_min()` and pop both stay O(1), since popping automatically reveals the correct prior minimum without any recomputation
It reduces the stack's memory usage compared to storing values alone
It's required so the stack can support values of different data types
Computing the minimum on demand would make push, not get_min, slower
mcqs.explanation: Scanning for the minimum on every `get_min()` call would be O(n) per call, which defeats the purpose; storing each entry's own minimum snapshot means popping naturally exposes the previous correct minimum with zero extra work. This approach uses more memory per entry, not less, has nothing to do with supporting mixed data types, and it's `get_min` that would become slow under the naive approach, not push.

mcqs.question: Why is the pairs-on-one-stack min-stack design usually easier to implement correctly than a separate auxiliary min-stack?
options: It has better time complexity for get_min
Auxiliary min-stacks can't achieve O(1) get_min
The pairs version stores less data overall than any auxiliary-stack variant
There's only one structure to keep synchronized, removing the risk of the two stacks drifting out of sync when pushes and pops aren't mirrored correctly
mcqs.explanation: Both designs achieve O(1) on every operation — the difference is implementation risk, not asymptotic complexity: a two-structure design can go subtly wrong if pops aren't applied to both stacks in lockstep, a mistake impossible by construction in the single-structure pairs version. The pairs version actually stores more data per entry (two values instead of one), not less.

mcqs.question: A circular queue tracks only front and rear indices, with no size counter. Why can this fail to distinguish an empty queue from a full one?
options: Both an empty queue and a full queue can end up with front equal to rear, since rear wraps around to meet front exactly when the buffer is full
A circular queue can never become full by design
Front and rear indices are never equal in a circular queue
This only happens if the queue's capacity is an odd number
mcqs.explanation: The wraparound behavior that makes a circular buffer space-efficient also creates this exact ambiguity: filling the buffer completely makes rear catch back up to front, producing the identical index relationship an empty queue has. It isn't tied to capacity parity, a circular queue absolutely can become full, and front/rear being equal is a real, recurring state, not an impossibility.

mcqs.question: Combining a min-stack with a batched "increment the bottom k elements" operation, what goes wrong if the batch increment doesn't also update the cached per-entry minimums?
options: Nothing — cached minimums are automatically recomputed whenever get_min is called
The increment operation would fail to execute at all
The stack's push operation would stop being O(1)
The cached minimum for affected entries can become stale — too low — since it reflects pre-increment values that have since changed without going through the normal push path
mcqs.explanation: The min-stack pattern computes each entry's minimum snapshot at push time; a batch increment changes stored values later, outside that mechanism, so any minimum computed before the batch update can silently understate the true current minimum unless explicitly recomputed. Nothing here recomputes minimums automatically, the increment itself still executes fine, and push's complexity is unaffected — the issue is purely the staleness of previously cached minimum values.
